ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain synaptic connectomes supply a natural graph for sensorimotor flow, but they have rarely been used as the policy network that actually moves an embodied body.
ocar.challenge: Deep-RL locomotion controllers usually rely on hand-crafted MLPs that are hard to relate to real circuits, while connectome-constrained models have mostly stayed in simplified sensory or premotor subsystems.
ocar.action: On arXiv (2026), Jin, Zhu, Zhang, and Sui introduce the Fly-connectomic Graph Model (FlyGM): they instantiate the adult Drosophila FlyWire connectome as an unweighted directed graph controller for a simulated biomechanical fly and train it with deep reinforcement learning.
ocar.resolution: FlyGM achieves stable performance on diverse locomotion tasks with better sample efficiency than graph and non-graph baselines. Class-wise information-flow patterns match experimental neuroscience more than an Erdős–Rényi control, so the authors argue wiring diagrams can serve as functional closed-loop controllers.
ocar.future_work: They flag richer synapse counts and neurotransmitter or sex-specific annotations, higher per-step compute than MLPs, and tests beyond locomotion as next steps.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly wiring diagram is turned into the “brain” of a simulated fly that learns to walk and turn. The connectome-shaped controller learns more efficiently than generic networks and makes the flow of information easier to interpret.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2026; v3 dated 14 June 2026), Jin and colleagues present FlyGM, a graph-structured RL policy that directly uses the adult Drosophila whole-brain connectome to control a simulated biomechanical fly. Even as an unweighted directed graph without synapse counts or transmitter types, the architecture yields stable locomotion and better sample efficiency than graph and non-graph baselines. Dynamic information flow is more class-differentiated than on a random Erdős–Rényi graph. The project page is https://lnsgroup.cc/research/FlyGM.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion is qualitative on task scores; numeric returns are not given here. Sufficiency of an unweighted graph is an authorship claim for this simulated body, not a statement that synapse weights are biologically irrelevant. Alignment with experimental findings is described as consistency of flow patterns, not a quantitative match to recorded spike trains. Per-step compute and memory exceed MLP controllers.

plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly wiring diagram is turned into the “brain” of a simulated fly that learns to walk and turn. The connectome-shaped controller learns more efficiently than generic networks and makes the flow of information easier to interpret.

ocar.opportunity: Brain networks nest small dense modules inside larger ones, a hierarchical modular layout that is thought to balance specialized processing with global integration.
ocar.challenge: How that hierarchy shapes computation, as opposed to simple modularity or random wiring, has been hard to isolate.
ocar.action: In a Nature Communications article in press (accepted June 2026), Milisav, Luppi, Suárez, Lajoie, and Mišić generate multi-level hierarchical modular networks with a blockmodel, run them as recurrent reservoirs, and compare memory, multitasking, and timescales against strictly modular, random, and empirical human structural connectomes, including a hierarchy-preserving null and MEG timescales.
ocar.resolution: Hierarchical modular reservoirs enhance memory capacity, support multitasking, and produce a broader range of temporal dynamics, advantages they trace to reciprocal and cyclic motifs. Hierarchy-preserving nulls isolate a positive effect of empirical hierarchical modularity on memory, and hierarchical organization helps shape brain-like MEG timescales.
ocar.future_work: The paper is an unedited article-in-press; the authors position the results as guidance for neuromorphic architecture design rather than a finished hardware implementation.

summaries.beginner: Brains are organized as nested clusters of clusters. This study builds artificial networks with that nested layout and shows they remember better, juggle more tasks, and produce more brain-like timing than flatter or random networks.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026, article in press; received August 2025, accepted 5 June 2026), Milisav and colleagues implement hierarchical modular blockmodels as RNN reservoirs. Hierarchical networks outperform strictly modular and random graphs on memory capacity, multitasking, and temporal-dynamic range, with advantages linked to reciprocal and cyclic motifs. A hierarchical modularity-preserving null isolates a positive effect of empirical human structural hierarchy on memory, and reservoir timescales are compared to MEG-derived brain timescales. The work is framed as insight for neuromorphic computing.
summaries.advanced: This extract is an unedited in-press PDF; copy may still change. Memory-capacity values visible in a figure panel are not restated as a single headline number in the selected text. Benefits are shown in reservoirs, not in a trained feed-forward classifier. Empirical tests use human structural connectivity and MEG timescales, not synaptic-resolution animal connectomes.

plain_language_summary: Brains are organized as nested clusters of clusters. This study builds artificial networks with that nested layout and shows they remember better, juggle more tasks, and produce more brain-like timing than flatter or random networks.

ocar.opportunity: Human color vision starts in the fovea, where L, M, and S cone signals are compared, but the synaptic wiring of those comparisons has been inferred largely from nonhuman primates.
ocar.challenge: Linking macaque cone-opponent pathways (midget L vs. M; small-bistratified S vs. L+M) to human trichromatic mechanisms has been difficult because human foveal circuits were not reconstructed at connectomic resolution.
ocar.action: In PNAS (2024), Kim, Packer, and Dacey reconstruct color-coding pathways from the foveal S-ON (blue-cone) bipolar with serial block-face SEM of human central retina at three eccentricities (~200, ~300, and ~600 µm; voxels 5×5×50 nm), skeletonized in TrakEM2, plus supporting macaque physiology.
ocar.resolution: S-ON bipolar cells contact not only small bistratified ganglion cells but also a large bistratified type and a subpopulation of ON-midget ganglion cells that also receive L vs. M midget bipolar input, defining an excitatory motif that merges cardinal red–green and blue–yellow circuits at the first stage of human vision.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue complete human foveal wiring diagrams are within reach; physiology in this extract is from macaque, and tissue was medically unremarkable at enucleation.

summaries.beginner: Color vision starts when the eye compares three kinds of cone cells. This team maps those comparisons in the human fovea and finds that the classic “red–green” and “blue–yellow” paths already mix in an excitatory circuit, which may help explain trichromatic color.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2024), Kim, Packer, and Dacey apply connectomic reconstruction to human foveal retina, tracing excitatory outputs of the S-ON bipolar to small bistratified, large bistratified, and a subset of ON-midget ganglion cells. Volumes at ~200, ~300, and ~600 µm eccentricity were imaged by SBEM (5×5×50 nm) and reconstructed in TrakEM2. The merged motif is proposed as a candidate for trichromatic cone opponency at the retinal first stage. Loose-patch chromatic responses shown in the paper come from macaque retina, not the human EM volumes.
summaries.advanced: Catalog tags list mouse retina; the paper is human (and macaque physiology). “Singular role” in trichromatic vision is a proposed function of the motif, not a perceptual experiment. Ribbon counts and connectivity were confirmed with multiple annotators, but completeness of the foveal diagram is prospective. Ocular status was medically unremarkable at enucleation; eccentricity sampling is three locations, not a continuous map.

plain_language_summary: Color vision starts when the eye compares three kinds of cone cells. This team maps those comparisons in the human fovea and finds that the classic “red–green” and “blue–yellow” paths already mix in an excitatory circuit, which may help explain trichromatic color.

ocar.opportunity: Vision must detect intensity changes even when optics and self-motion blur edges, so early circuits that sharpen contrast would be widely useful.
ocar.challenge: First-order interneurons L1 and L2 in Drosophila show unusual biphasic flash responses whose second phase can be larger than the first, which is not a simple linear differentiator.
ocar.action: In Current Biology (published 20 January 2025), Pang, Chen, Xie, Druckmann, Clandinin, and Yang combine in vivo two-photon voltage imaging, genetic circuit dissection, and a dynamical model of recurrent feedback, then test the model on moving natural images and L2 responses.
ocar.resolution: Recurrent circuitry shapes the second phase of L1/L2 responses; the model shows feedback speeds contrast responses and compensates motion blur, and L2 follows the model’s sharpening on naturalistic stimuli. Octopaminergic modulation can retune the feedback to expected self-motion blur.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose the motif as a general, context-tunable way to enhance salient changes; they note L1/L2 responses are nonlinear (light vs. dark flashes differ) and also shaped by photoreceptor adaptation and lateral interactions.

summaries.beginner: When a fly moves, the world blurs, yet it still needs sharp edges. This study shows that early visual cells use a feedback loop to sharpen contrast over time, and that the loop can be retuned when the fly is more active.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Biology (2025; 35:333–346.e6; DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2024.11.064), Pang and colleagues measure L1 and L2 temporal filters with two-photon voltage imaging. Biphasic dark-flash responses have a second phase often larger in area than the first; genetic isolation shows recurrent feedback sculpts that phase. A dynamical model fit to impulse responses predicts faster, sharpened responses to moving natural scenes, matching L2, with octopamine as a proposed gain on expected blur. Light and dark flashes are not linear inverses.
summaries.advanced: This PMC author manuscript is the published 2025 article (catalog year 2024). “About 40%” style numeric filter parameters are not quoted in the selected extract. The claim of generality beyond fly vision is proposed, not demonstrated. Prior photoreceptor biophysics still contribute; the new point is recurrent circuit feedback on top of that.

plain_language_summary: When a fly moves, the world blurs, yet it still needs sharp edges. This study shows that early visual cells use a feedback loop to sharpen contrast over time, and that the loop can be retuned when the fly is more active.

ocar.opportunity: Dense staining and fast light-sheet imaging can now capture individual axons over large human samples, a mesoscale gap between diffusion MRI and synaptic EM.
ocar.challenge: Serial-section fluorescence volumes at petavoxel scale must be montaged, aligned through cutting deformation, and traced as continuous axons—problems that image-based stitching alone does not solve.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (this extract posted 1 April 2026), Torres, Takasaki, Gliko, Laughland, Yu, Turschak, Hellevik, Balaram, Perlman, Silversmith, Collman, Sümbül, and Reid describe a modular pipeline that uses ML segmentation to drive stitching, alignment, and automated tracing of densely labeled axons across centimeter-scale serial sections.
ocar.resolution: They validate segmentation-driven assembly of individual axons over centimeter-scale sections and show traces used for local orientation analysis and proofreading on aligned volumes, aiming at whole-human-brain mesoscale “axonal connectomics” together with expansion and light-sheet methods (Turschak et al. 2026).
ocar.future_work: NIH awards R01MH117820, UG3MH126864, and UM1NS132207 are acknowledged; the pipeline is presented as enabling, not as a completed whole-brain map. The extract’s discussion runs into the reference list, so quantitative error rates are not captured here.

summaries.beginner: Mapping single axons across a whole human brain is still out of reach for electron microscopy. This computational pipeline stitches serial light-microscope sections by following the axons themselves so long-range fibers can be traced at mesoscale.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (DOI 10.1101/2024.06.11.598365; version posted 1 April 2026), Torres and colleagues at the Allen Institute present a scalable pipeline for axonal connectomics: ML segmentation of densely stained axons, then segmentation-driven stitching and alignment across serial sections, plus automated tracing. They report validation on centimeter-scale human sections and use traces for local orientation and proofreading. The experimental partner methods are light-sheet fluorescence and tissue expansion (Turschak et al. 2026). The goal is mesoscale connectivity over the whole human brain, complementary to dMRI and EM.
summaries.advanced: This extract is a 2026 update of a 2024 preprint, not a journal article. Quantitative tracing accuracy, false-merge rates, and dataset size in millimeters of axon are not stated in the selected text. “Should enable” whole-brain studies is prospective. Ground truth and proofreading are credited to Hellevik; details of the test volumes are not in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Mapping single axons across a whole human brain is still out of reach for electron microscopy. This computational pipeline stitches serial light-microscope sections by following the axons themselves so long-range fibers can be traced at mesoscale.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics increasingly analyzes weighted graphs whose edge weights span many orders of magnitude, so null models should preserve weighted degree (strength), not only binary degree.
ocar.challenge: Maslov–Sneppen-style rewiring still dominates, which can mis-attribute higher-order features such as rich clubs when weights are ignored.
ocar.action: In Nature Computational Science (published 10 December 2024), Milisav, Bazinet, Betzel, and Mišić introduce a simulated-annealing procedure that randomizes networks while preserving strength sequences, including directed and signed graphs, and they inspect ensemble variability in morphospace.
ocar.resolution: The annealer outperforms other rewiring algorithms at strength preservation and generalizes across formats and real-world networks. Accurate strength preservation changes inferences about brain organization, including the rich-club phenomenon, relative to binary-degree nulls.
ocar.future_work: They lay out best practices for choosing rewiring algorithms on next-generation weighted connectomes; graph measures tested on consensus structural networks include weighted clustering, path length, and rich-club coefficient (HCP and Lausanne processing cited in reporting tables).

summaries.beginner: To tell whether a brain-network pattern is special, scientists scramble the network and look again. This paper’s scramble keeps each region’s total connection strength, which can change conclusions about hubs compared with older methods that only count links.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Computational Science (2024; DOI 10.1038/s43588-024-00735-z), Milisav and colleagues propose simulated annealing to generate strength-preserving randomized networks. The method outperforms common rewiring algorithms, extends to directed and signed networks, and uses morphospace plots to assess ensemble variability. On weighted group-consensus structural connectomes, null-model choice alters inferences such as the rich-club. Tests use Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney comparisons of strength preservation and graph measures.
summaries.advanced: Catalog metadata list bioRxiv; the extract is the journal article. The selected PDF’s later pages are reporting checklists rather than the full results tables, so per-dataset p-values are not quoted here. “Fundamentally different inferences” is demonstrated for established features such as the rich club, not for every graph statistic. Applicability beyond neuroscience is claimed via diverse real-world networks in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: To tell whether a brain-network pattern is special, scientists scramble the network and look again. This paper’s scramble keeps each region’s total connection strength, which can change conclusions about hubs compared with older methods that only count links.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila have ~10× fewer neurons than adults and a synaptic-resolution mushroom-body connectome, so they are a place to test which learning computations a simplified circuit can support.
ocar.challenge: More than half of mushroom-body connection classes were unexpected from earlier work; it is unclear whether larvae can perform cognitive tasks beyond simple odor–reward association.
ocar.action: In Learning & Memory (2024), Sen, El-Keredy, Jacob, Mancini, Asnaz, Widmann, Gerber, and Thoener test larvae on conditioned inhibition, sensory preconditioning, and second-order conditioning using odor–sugar paradigms.
ocar.resolution: They find evidence for conditioned inhibition, as in adult flies and honeybees, but not for sensory preconditioning or second-order conditioning. Control experiments show association formation during the conditioning phase was effective regardless of preconditioning treatment.
ocar.future_work: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: they list protocol changes (trial number, odors, reinforcers, video tracking) that might reveal the missing forms, then discuss four larval-brain organization hypotheses if the gap is real.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae can learn that a smell predicts no reward, a slightly more complex trick than simple pairing. They did not, in these tests, show two other forms of higher-order learning that adult flies and bees can do.
summaries.intermediate: In Learning & Memory (2024), Sen and colleagues probe larval Drosophila with three tasks that go beyond simple associative learning. Conditioned inhibition is supported; sensory preconditioning and second-order conditioning are not, unlike reports in adult flies and honeybees. A control (their Figure 6) shows PAIRED versus UNPAIRED conditioning still produces memory after either compound or separated preconditioning, so failure is not from a dead conditioning phase. They discuss life-history and circuit-simplification explanations with explicit caveats.
summaries.advanced: The authors stress that null results do not prove incapacity. Connectomic motivation cites Eichler et al. 2017 and Winding et al. 2023; this paper is behavioral, not a new EM volume. Statistical details live in Supplemental Table S1, not fully in the selected extract. Catalog method tags include electron microscopy because of the framing, not because new EM is presented.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae can learn that a smell predicts no reward, a slightly more complex trick than simple pairing. They did not, in these tests, show two other forms of higher-order learning that adult flies and bees can do.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome projects aim to explain brain function from synaptic-scale maps in C. elegans, mouse, and human, and popular reviews have celebrated that structural progress.
ocar.challenge: The authors argue those projects and an Eisenstein review omit the neural extracellular matrix / perineuronal net (nECM/PNN) that surrounds neurons, so “naked neuron” wiring diagrams cannot explain mentality.
ocar.action: In International Journal of Psychiatry Research (2024), Marx and Gilon review staining, TEM/SEM, and mass-spectrometry evidence for nECM/PNN and restate their tripartite memory hypothesis in which cognitive units of information (cuinfo) are metal-centered complexes in the matrix that bind neurotransmitters.
ocar.resolution: They conclude connectomics without the matrix cannot formulate a credible mechanism of memory, emotion, or consciousness, analogizing mentality to a “neural event horizon” beyond maps and numbers.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a hypothesis-driven critique, not new ultrastructural data; it calls for a paradigm that includes nECM/PNN biochemistry rather than specifying a connectomic experiment.

summaries.beginner: This commentary says wiring diagrams of synapses leave out the gel that wraps every neuron. The authors think memories may be stored as chemical complexes in that gel, so connectome maps alone cannot explain thoughts or feelings.
summaries.intermediate: In Int. J. Psychiatr. Res. (2024; 7(4):1–8), Marx and Gilon criticize connectome collaborations and an Eisenstein review for ignoring nECM/PNN, documented by lectin stains, EM, and proteomics. They summarize a prior tripartite model in which cuinfo metal–neurotransmitter complexes in the matrix encode emotive states. The paper is a review/hypothesis, not a methods or reconstruction study. C. elegans, mouse, and human projects are named as the targets of the critique.
summaries.advanced: This is not an empirical connectomics result; claims about cuinfo are the authors’ biochemical hypothesis. Tone is polemical (“myopia”). No new quantification of matrix or synapses is given. Venue is a psychiatry journal; the extract should be read as opinion relative to mainstream EM connectomics.

plain_language_summary: This commentary says wiring diagrams of synapses leave out the gel that wraps every neuron. The authors think memories may be stored as chemical complexes in that gel, so connectome maps alone cannot explain thoughts or feelings.

ocar.opportunity: Foraging flies switch between straight long-distance flight and local zig-zag saccades; a small descending network that can generate or suppress those turns would explain the switch.
ocar.challenge: Which descending neurons (DNs) actually command body saccades, and which cells can shut the network off, was not identified at cellular resolution.
ocar.action: In Current Biology (2024), Ros, Omoto, and Dickinson combine two-photon imaging, optogenetics, ablation, and fly connectomes to test DNae014 and DNb01 and the interneuron VES041.
ocar.resolution: Four DNs (excitatory DNae014 and inhibitory DNb01 on each side) appear sufficient as saccade-generating units projecting to flight motor neuropil. Connectome-identified VES041 inhibits all four; its activation strongly suppresses saccades, a candidate brake for straight flight during dispersal or odor surges.
ocar.future_work: Double ablation of both DN types in the same fly was not achieved; VES041’s GABAergic identity is machine-learning based and needs biochemical confirmation. Ablating either DN type alone does not abolish all turns.

summaries.beginner: Flying fruit flies make quick body turns when searching locally and fly straight when traveling far. This team finds four descending neurons that command the turns and a large inhibitory cell that can silence them.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2024; 34:531–540.e5), Ros, Omoto, and Dickinson show that DNae014 (excitatory) and DNb01 (inhibitory) form left and right saccade-generating units. Two-photon imaging links each cell’s activity one-to-one with rapid wing-motion changes; optogenetic activation evokes syndirectional turns; ablation lengthens straight-flight intervals. Using published connectomes they identify VES041, which inhibits all four command neurons; activating it strongly suppresses saccades. Driver lines for VES041 were generated for this work.
summaries.advanced: “Only four descending neurons appear sufficient” is the authors’ reading of imaging, activation, and partial ablation—not a proof that no other DNs contribute. Remaining slower saccades after single-type ablation imply redundancy or partial motor programs. Transmitter of VES041 is a prediction. Catalog datasets mention FANC/MANC VNC; the paper uses recently published fly connectomes plus new physiology.

plain_language_summary: Flying fruit flies make quick body turns when searching locally and fly straight when traveling far. This team finds four descending neurons that command the turns and a large inhibitory cell that can silence them.

ocar.opportunity: Machine-learning networks suggest that a simple excitatory–inhibitory XOR motif could supply both a discrepancy signal (a loss) and a homeostatic brake on excess input.
ocar.challenge: Whether that motif is common enough in real connectomes to be a conserved plasticity primitive, and whether homeostasis alone could drive relevant biological learning, is speculative.
ocar.action: In a brief arXiv commentary (2024), J. M. D. Lucas proposes a four-to-one excitatory-to-inhibitory XOR motif as a basis for plasticity and winner-take-all patterns, then counts its occurrence in published C. elegans, Drosophila neuropil, and mouse V1 connectomes.
ocar.resolution: The catalog abstract reports motif counts ranging from tens (C. elegans) to millions (several Drosophila neuropils) to more than tens of millions (mouse V1). If validated, architecture and loss would be identified; plasticity would be framed as a regulatory system conserved across complexity.
ocar.future_work: The hypothesis requires experimental validation; the piece does not demonstrate that the counted subgraphs implement XOR computation or that homeostasis is sufficient for learning.

summaries.beginner: This short commentary asks whether a tiny mix of “on” and “off” connections, like an XOR logic gate, is a repeated motif from worms to mice. Counting it in published wiring diagrams, the author suggests homeostasis alone might steer learning.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2024; catalog DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2412.20090), Lucas speculates that a neural XOR motif with a 4:1 excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio could implement a loss signal and halt surplus input, supporting winner-take-all dynamics. The abstract reports prevalence from tens of instances in C. elegans to millions in Drosophila neuropils and more than tens of millions in mouse V1. The argument is analogical to machine-learning architecture plus loss, with plasticity as evolved regulation.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file text is Vincent A. Cicirello, “Optimizing Genetic Algorithms Using the Binomial Distribution” (arXiv:2412.02009), a GA runtime paper, not Lucas 2024. Summaries use the catalog abstract only; motif counts were not verified in matching PDF. XOR function of counted subgraphs is hypothesized, not shown physiologically.

plain_language_summary: This short commentary asks whether a tiny mix of “on” and “off” connections, like an XOR logic gate, is a repeated motif from worms to mice. Counting it in published wiring diagrams, the author suggests homeostasis alone might steer learning.

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM reconstructions of neural and glial ultrastructure are scientifically rich but hard to share, teach, and inspect collaboratively in 3D.
ocar.challenge: Meshes from serial-section stacks must be built, combined with absorption/heatmap signals, and deployed in consumer VR/metaverse clients without losing nanometric context.
ocar.action: At ACM WEB3D ’24, Calì and Agus present NeuroVerse: a pipeline from volume-EM stacks through segmentation, mesh reconstruction, and heatmap computation, optimized for Spatial.io, including a virtual anatomy lab.
ocar.resolution: They report preliminary potential for neuroanatomy education, remote scientific collaboration, and broader access to ultrastructural data, with sessions on morphology–space correlation and neuroenergetic absorption models.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include lack of interactive volume transparency for overlapping interiors and manual marker-based registration of scene parts. Future work includes controlled education studies and ingesting automatic reconstructions and mesoscale light-microscopy models.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope reconstructions of brain cells are usually stuck on a scientist’s computer. This project puts those 3D models into a shared virtual-reality space so students and labs can walk around them together.
summaries.intermediate: In The 29th International ACM Conference on 3D Web Technology (WEB3D ’24, Guimarães; DOI 10.1145/3665318.3677154), Calì and Agus describe NeuroVerse, a framework that turns volume-EM image stacks into VR-ready meshes plus absorption heatmaps for the Spatial.io ecosystem. Contributions include a virtual anatomy lab and collaborative analysis of ultrastructure and neuroenergetic maps. Results are described as preliminary. Limitations listed are interactive transparency and automatic multi-part registration.
summaries.advanced: No quantitative learning-outcome trial is in this extract; education benefits are prospective. The pipeline is a visualization/deployment stack, not a new segmentation algorithm. Catalog stages include segmentation because meshes are produced from EM stacks; the paper’s novelty is immersive delivery. Automatic reconstruction integration is future work (citing Schmidt, Svara, Xu).

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope reconstructions of brain cells are usually stuck on a scientist’s computer. This project puts those 3D models into a shared virtual-reality space so students and labs can walk around them together.

ocar.opportunity: Dust-evoked grooming in Drosophila is a prioritized sequence across the body; a synaptic map of head bristle mechanosensory neurons (BMNs) would show how parallel pathways encode location and sequence.
ocar.challenge: Head BMNs were among the least described insect mechanosensors, and no complete synaptic-resolution somatotopic map of a head existed.
ocar.action: In eLife (2024, version 2), Eichler, Hampel, Alejandro-García, Calle-Schuler, Santana-Cruz, Kmecova, Blagburn, Hoopfer, and Seeds combine dye fills, new driver lines, and FAFB/FlyWire reconstruction to map nearly all head BMNs from periphery to brain arbors.
ocar.resolution: Individual BMNs elicit aimed grooming of specific head sites and together a whole-head sequence, yielding the first synaptic-resolution somatotopic map of a head and defining parallel pathways. eLife rates the work valuable with solid data and community resources.
ocar.future_work: PoOc and Su bristle innervation remains uncertain; BMN transmitter (acetylcholine vs. histamine) is unresolved despite cholinergic ML predictions. Unknown sensory neurons in FAFB may fill gaps.

summaries.beginner: Flies wipe dust off their heads in a set order. This team maps almost all of the touch sensors on the fly head into the brain, showing that each patch of bristles has its own path and that together they can trigger the full wiping sequence.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2024; 10.7554/eLife.87602.2), Eichler and colleagues reconstruct head bristle mechanosensory neurons with dye fills, transgenic lines, and the FAFB EM volume (FlyWire). Individually, BMNs drive location-aimed grooming; collectively they drive a whole-head sequence, supporting a parallel model of action selection. The map is described as the most comprehensive BMN description for any Drosophila body part. Related FAFB work covers JO neurons (prior CATMAID) and taste-peg mechanosensors (38 reconstructed here).
summaries.advanced: eLife assessment calls the description near-complete and the data solid, not a full causal proof of the parallel-suppression model. Some bristle classes lack confirmed BMNs. Neurotransmitter is not settled. Catalog dimension is proofreading because of EM reconstruction/annotation in FAFB.

plain_language_summary: Flies wipe dust off their heads in a set order. This team maps almost all of the touch sensors on the fly head into the brain, showing that each patch of bristles has its own path and that together they can trigger the full wiping sequence.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy now yields complete neurite wiring in large tissue blocks and entire nervous systems, but morphology alone cannot assign molecular identity.
ocar.challenge: Structural connectomics identifies elements by shape; linking those reconstructions to genes, probes, and other modalities is needed to interpret specific circuits such as basal-ganglia dopamine networks.
ocar.action: In Neurosciences Research (2024), Ohno, Karube, and Fujiyama review volume-EM advances together with EM-visible probes and correlative methods that place molecules and gene expression into the same ultrastructural context.
ocar.resolution: The catalog abstract argues these tools will clarify interactions of defined neurons and may reveal new aspects of basal-ganglia circuitry involving dopamine neurons and adaptive change.
ocar.future_work: The review points to expected mechanistic insight rather than presenting a new volume or quantified circuit.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps see shape but not always which genes a cell expresses. This review covers new labels and combined-microscope methods meant to put molecular identity into those 3D maps, including circuits that use dopamine.
summaries.intermediate: In Neurosciences Research (2024; DOI 10.1016/j.neures.2024.06.002), Ohno, Karube, and Fujiyama review volume EM’s expanded scale and its morphological limits, then survey probes visible in EM and correlative multi-modal integration. The intended payoff is genetically and molecularly defined circuits, with basal-ganglia dopamine networks as an example. The piece is a review of tools and prospects, not a primary reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is Ezure, Matsuzaki, Urakubo, and Ohno, Scientific Reports, on SBF-SEM of human facial skin and arrector pili muscle—not the catalog Neuroscience Research review. Summaries use the catalog abstract only. Shared last author (Ohno) does not make the PDFs the same paper.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps see shape but not always which genes a cell expresses. This review covers new labels and combined-microscope methods meant to put molecular identity into those 3D maps, including circuits that use dopamine.

ocar.opportunity: A 1998 Learning & Memory special issue framed insect mushroom bodies as the place to understand circuit-level coding; 25 years of tools now make that program feasible.
ocar.challenge: Molecular and coarse imaging advances had outrun circuit physiology; without circuit operation, brain function would remain incomplete.
ocar.action: In a 2024 Learning & Memory editorial, Fiala and Kaun introduce a new special issue, surveying connectomes, genetic reagents, and in vivo circuit work that turned the mushroom body into a model for sensory encoding, memory, and choice.
ocar.resolution: They credit community connectomes and shared genetic tools, and they expect further technology and collaboration to generalize insights to other structures and species.
ocar.future_work: The editorial is a field synthesis, not new data; it points readers to the accompanying articles (including Sen et al. on larval cognitive limits in the same issue).

summaries.beginner: Twenty-five years after a landmark journal issue, this editorial says the insect mushroom body is now a working circuit diagram for learning. Shared wiring maps and genetic tools, not only new molecules, made that possible.
summaries.intermediate: In Learning & Memory (2024; Vol. 31, No. 5, a053827.123), Fiala and Kaun revisit Heisenberg’s 1998 gap—circuit function between molecules and behavior—and argue mushroom bodies now fill it via connectomes (e.g., adult Drosophila central brain) and in vivo circuit methods. The editorial introduces a special issue on mushroom-body progress. Historical notes include Dujardin (1850) and arthropod conservation of the structure.
summaries.advanced: This is an editorial, not an empirical connectome. Generalization to other brains is aspirational. Receipt/acceptance dates are 21–22 April 2024. Catalog axis is biological_application; there is no new dataset.

plain_language_summary: Twenty-five years after a landmark journal issue, this editorial says the insect mushroom body is now a working circuit diagram for learning. Shared wiring maps and genetic tools, not only new molecules, made that possible.

ocar.opportunity: Network motifs are candidate computational building blocks, but standard over-representation tests struggle to compare motifs, handle correlations, and choose a null model.
ocar.challenge: Thousands of possible larger subgraphs make Bonferroni-corrected p-values impractical, and motif counts are not independent.
ocar.action: Bénichou, Masson, and Vestergaard develop lossless compression via subgraph contraction, treating motif-set inference as MDL model selection, then apply it to synaptic-resolution neural networks for comparative connectomics (arXiv v2 11 Oct 2024; PLoS Comput. Biol. catalog DOI).
ocar.resolution: The framework selects a collectively most compressive motif set without an a priori null, inherently accounting for multiple testing and subgraph correlations. They validate on numerical data and characterize inferred circuit motifs and compressibility of biological connectomes.
ocar.future_work: Figure 5 in the extract compares density, reciprocity, cycles, and symmetry of inferred motif sets versus density-matched random graphlets; biological interpretation of those averages is left to the full paper’s connectome applications.

summaries.beginner: Instead of asking whether a little wiring pattern is “surprisingly common,” this method asks which set of patterns best compresses the network. That gives a fairer way to compare motifs in real brain wiring diagrams.
summaries.intermediate: In work appearing as PLoS Computational Biology (DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012460; this extract is arXiv:2311.16308v2, 11 Oct 2024), Bénichou, Masson, and Vestergaard infer motif sets by lossless compression (subgraph contractions) under the MDL principle. The method avoids specifying a classical null and comparing isolated p-values. After numerical validation they apply it to synaptic-resolution neural networks as comparative connectomics. They illustrate topological summaries of inferred motif sets (density, reciprocity, cycles, graph-polynomial root).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s discussion does not name which animal connectomes were compressed or quote bits-saved numbers. “Guarantees robust statistical inference” is the authors’ claim for the MDL framing. Five-node Bonferroni arithmetic (~10,000 tests) is an illustration of why p-value motif mining fails, not a result of this method.

plain_language_summary: Instead of asking whether a little wiring pattern is “surprisingly common,” this method asks which set of patterns best compresses the network. That gives a fairer way to compare motifs in real brain wiring diagrams.

ocar.opportunity: Serotonin changes global behavior, but how receptor diversity maps onto a complete connectome and brain-wide dynamics is rarely knowable in one animal.
ocar.challenge: C. elegans releases serotonin (e.g., from NSM) to slow locomotion and increase feeding, yet which receptors, time courses, and neurons carry that modulation was incomplete.
ocar.action: In Cell (2023), Dag, Nwabudike, Kang, and Flavell colleagues combine comprehensive receptor genetics, whole-brain imaging in moving worms, and a map of serotonin-receptor expression onto the connectome.
ocar.resolution: MOD-1, SER-4, and LGC-50 are core receptors for slowing on serotonin release; SER-1/5/7 interact. SER-4 responds to sudden increases and MOD-1 to persistent release. Serotonin-associated dynamics span many behavioral networks, and receptor sites plus synapses help predict which neurons covary with NSM.
ocar.future_work: Methods in the extract detail shuffle controls for NSM–behavior correlations given long autocorrelation; the paper maps organization rather than claiming a full causal simulation of every modulated neuron.

summaries.beginner: Serotonin makes a worm slow down and eat more, but it hits many receptors across the brain. This study names the key receptors, watches the whole brain, and shows how the wiring diagram plus receptor locations predict which cells join in.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2023; 186:2574–2592.e20), Dag, Nwabudike, Kang, Gomes, Kim, Atanas, Bueno, Estrem, Pugliese, Wang, Towlson, and Flavell dissect C. elegans serotonergic foraging. Genetics identify MOD-1, SER-4, and LGC-50 as core for slow locomotion, with SER-1, SER-5, and SER-7 as modulators; SER-4 versus MOD-1 split transient versus persistent release. Whole-brain imaging shows widespread serotonin-associated activity. Mapping all receptor-expression sites onto the connectome, with synaptic connectivity, helps predict serotonin-associated neurons.
summaries.advanced: “Typically >30” neuromodulatory networks is from a different paper in this shard (zebrafish); this paper’s extract does not quote that figure. NSM–behavior tests use encoding-model shuffle controls because temporal shifting is underpowered given >100 s autocorrelation. Catalog dataset is the White+ C. elegans connectome used as the anatomical scaffold, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: Serotonin makes a worm slow down and eat more, but it hits many receptors across the brain. This study names the key receptors, watches the whole brain, and shows how the wiring diagram plus receptor locations predict which cells join in.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks rarely copy a real connectome’s topology; a complete small wiring diagram such as C. elegans could be a bio-plausible architecture prior.
ocar.challenge: Prior “deep connectomic networks” used small-world inspiration without one-to-one tensor copies of living synapses and neuron classes.
ocar.action: In a 2023 arXiv/bioRxiv report, Bardozzo, Terlizzi, Liò, and Tagliaferri introduce ElegansNet: nearly 1:1 maps of C. elegans neurons and synapses into tensors, preserving sensor/interneuron/motor organization, compared with random wiring, Watts–Strogatz nets, and standard vision models.
ocar.resolution: ElegansNet outperforms random wiring and, on reported validation sets, reaches top-1 accuracy of 99.99% on CIFAR-10 and 99.84% on unsupervised MNIST, competitive with transformers and attention autoencoders in the authors’ benchmarks.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s later pages are references; independent replication and whether accuracy reflects topology versus capacity/training protocol should be checked in the full methods.

summaries.beginner: Researchers copy the worm’s wiring diagram into a deep network for image tasks. They report that this bio-shaped net beats randomly rewired copies and scores extremely high on standard vision benchmarks.
summaries.intermediate: In a brief 2023 report (arXiv:2304.13538; catalog bioRxiv 10.1101/2023.04.23.537987), Bardozzo and colleagues transform the C. elegans connectome into learnable tensors (ElegansNet), keeping functional class layout. It beats randomly wired controls and performs similarly only to Watts–Strogatz small-world nets among those controls. Versus listed SOTA models they report 99.99% top-1 on CIFAR-10 and 99.84% on unsupervised MNIST validation. The goal is to study topology–learning interplay rather than nematode behavior.
summaries.advanced: Headline accuracies are extraordinary and come from the authors’ validation protocol in this extract; they should be read cautiously without the full training details. Catalog journal is bioRxiv; this PDF is the arXiv CS report. Tasks are image classification/reconstruction, not C. elegans behavior. Similarity to Watts–Strogatz is described as “slightly similar,” not identity.

plain_language_summary: Researchers copy the worm’s wiring diagram into a deep network for image tasks. They report that this bio-shaped net beats randomly rewired copies and scores extremely high on standard vision benchmarks.

ocar.opportunity: Direction-selective motion vision is a tractable neural computation; Drosophila genetics plus a visual-system connectome now specify the circuit in unusual molecular detail.
ocar.challenge: Blocking individual input neurons to T4/T5 is hard to interpret because those neurons also connect among themselves, changing the remaining inputs.
ocar.action: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2023), Borst and Groschner synthesize identity, morphology, synapses, transmitters, receptors, subcellular localization, and visual responses into a biophysically realistic account of fly motion detection, including multiplicative disinhibition.
ocar.resolution: The review presents an integrated picture of how T4/T5 direction selectivity is computed at moderate complexity. They recommend synapse-specific interventions (e.g., GluClα knockdown for Mi9→T4) or simulations when cell-wide blocks are ambiguous.
ocar.future_work: A method to block only the synapses from a given input onto T4/T5, sparing that cell’s other outputs, is not yet available.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies are a showcase for how brains detect which way things move. This review gathers the cells, chemicals, and wiring that compute motion and explains why simply shutting off one input cell can be misleading.
summaries.intermediate: In Annu. Rev. Neurosci. (2023; 46:17–37), Borst and Groschner review Drosophila motion vision as a model computation enabled by genetics and the visual connectome. The account includes neuron identity, morphology, connectivity, transmitters/receptors and their localization, plus membrane responses, supporting a biophysical circuit model. They discuss limits of blocking experiments given inter-input connectivity (Shinomiya et al. 2019) and point to receptor knockdown (Groschner et al. 2022 on Mi9/GluClα) or simulation as cleaner tests.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not new EM. The selected extract is front-plus-discussion; mid-review quantitative circuit numbers are not in the captured text. Multiplicative disinhibition is a keyword/theme of the review. Authors declare no competing interests. Catalog DOI matches 10.1146/annurev-neuro-080422-111929.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies are a showcase for how brains detect which way things move. This review gathers the cells, chemicals, and wiring that compute motion and explains why simply shutting off one input cell can be misleading.

ocar.opportunity: Assigning synaptic partners in large connectomes is still laborious if models only look at local EM appearance and ignore graph topology.
ocar.challenge: Most known connections are a tiny fraction of possible pairs, so a model must extrapolate from scarce labels using global connectivity structure.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2023), Wan, Liao, Zhao, Wang, Pan, and Du propose NCPNet, a GNN that jointly learns node and neighborhood features to score neuron-level links, trained on a small random subset of one connectome.
ocar.resolution: With 5% known connections, they report 91.88% accuracy on a Drosophila connectome and 93.79% on C. elegans. Kenyon-cell embeddings separate neuronal subtypes. Code: https://github.com/mxz12119/NCPNet.
ocar.future_work: They argue the model could speed synaptic partner assignment versus image-based detectors; the extract does not report precision–recall on withheld animals or EM-volume transfer.

summaries.beginner: Once some of a brain’s connections are known, a graph network tries to guess the rest from who is already linked to whom. The authors report high accuracy on fly and worm wiring diagrams using only a small fraction of known links.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2 July 2023; 10.1101/2023.06.29.547138), Wan and colleagues introduce NCPNet to infer neuron-level connections from topology rather than local synapse appearance. Trained on a small random subset of a single circuit, it reports 91.88% accuracy on Drosophila and 93.79% on C. elegans at 5% observed connections. Qualitative analysis of Kenyon-cell representations suggests subtype-discriminative features. They contrast this lightweight topological approach with compute-heavy volumetric CNNs.
summaries.advanced: Accuracy at 5% labels is the headline metric in this extract; class imbalance and whether “accuracy” equals edge-existence AUROC are not specified here. Training and testing on splits of one network can leak community structure. Catalog organism is elegans; evaluation also includes Drosophila. Not a substitute for EM synapse detection.

plain_language_summary: Once some of a brain’s connections are known, a graph network tries to guess the rest from who is already linked to whom. The authors report high accuracy on fly and worm wiring diagrams using only a small fraction of known links.

ocar.opportunity: Fifty years after the first fly olfactory shock-avoidance assay, combined behavior, molecules, physiology, systems methods, and first-generation EM connectomes make Drosophila a leading memory model.
ocar.challenge: The field needed a synthesis of the fifth research decade: mushroom-body output neurons, dopamine tiling, calyx microglomeruli, larval simplicity, CREB/Orb2, and active forgetting.
ocar.action: In Genetics FlyBook (2023), Ronald L. Davis reviews those advances and a model in which different dopamine populations and MBON balance assign appetitive versus aversive valence.
ocar.resolution: He highlights MBON compartments aligned with dopamine inputs, structural LTM changes in the calyx, larval learning as a simpler leading system, CREB and prion-like Orb2 in LTM, and pioneering work on permanent versus transient forgetting via memory-suppressor genes (e.g., PPL1/DAMB/Rac1 pathways).
ocar.future_work: Space limits omit disease models, metabolism, state dependence, and some higher-order learning; he expects another decade of concept extraction with the fly toolkit.

summaries.beginner: This review tours a decade of fruit-fly memory research: new output cells from the learning center, how dopamine writes good versus bad memories, and how the brain also actively forgets. Wiring diagrams now sit underneath those stories.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2023; 224:iyad085), Davis’s FlyBook chapter covers adult and larval EM connectomes as substrates for complete cue-to-behavior circuits. MBONs tile mushroom-body axon compartments in register with dopamine neuron inputs, supporting a valence-balance model. Calyx microglomeruli remodel with LTM. Molecular sections treat CREB and Orb2 oligomers. A two-path forgetting model (permanent vs. transient; PPL1 compartments, DAMB, Scribble/Rac1/Cofilin vs. intact PSD-LTM traces) is illustrated from Sabandal et al. 2021.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. “First-generation connectome” is Davis’s term for then-available adult/larval reconstructions. Forgetting mechanisms are synthesized from cited work, not new experiments here. Catalog stages list acquisition because of EM reconstruction’s role in the narrative.

plain_language_summary: This review tours a decade of fruit-fly memory research: new output cells from the learning center, how dopamine writes good versus bad memories, and how the brain also actively forgets. Wiring diagrams now sit underneath those stories.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit function depends on neuromodulation as well as synapses; a molecular map of GPCRs and cell types in adult zebrafish telencephalon would constrain that extra layer.
ocar.challenge: How combinatorial monoamine and neuropeptide systems weight each transcriptionally defined cell type, and how those types relate phylogenetically to other vertebrates, was unclear at high granularity.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (5 October 2023), Anneser, Satou, Hotz, and Friedrich combine bulk and deep single-cell transcriptomics with HCR spatial mapping of markers and GPCRs in adult zebrafish telencephalon.
ocar.resolution: They report 55 neuronal types mapped to telencephalic areas; every type is modulated by multiple monoamines and peptide combinations, typically >30 networks, but only a few diagnostic GPCRs at high level. SAMap alignments support conserved cell types with reptiles (bearded dragon) and other vertebrates, including Dl–hippocampus and Dc–isocortex links.
ocar.future_work: Dc cell types were not clearly split, possibly due to heterogeneity and low abundance; whether Dl’s posterior/medial–anterior/lateral molecular axis is functional remains unknown.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells are not only wired by synapses; they are also bathed in chemical messengers. This zebrafish atlas shows each cell type listens to many messengers but really “turns up” only a few, and some types look related to those in other vertebrates.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2023; 10.1101/2023.10.04.560846), Anneser and colleagues profile adult zebrafish telencephalon. Bulk sequencing distinguishes pallial subregions; scRNA-seq yields 55 neuronal types placed with HCR. Combinatorial GPCR logic implies all types receive multi-system modulation with unequal weights. Spatial maps refine Dp, Dl, Dm compartments (e.g., pDp vs. aDp). Phylogenetic SAMap links a subset of types to bearded dragon and, by extension, other vertebrates.
summaries.advanced: “Typically >30” networks per type is from the abstract; it is association of expression programs, not measured co-release. Volume EM is cited as the synaptic-diagram complement, not performed here. Catalog dataset DS15 zebrafish is transcriptomic/spatial, not a synapse map. Unedited preprint (October 2023).

plain_language_summary: Brain cells are not only wired by synapses; they are also bathed in chemical messengers. This zebrafish atlas shows each cell type listens to many messengers but really “turns up” only a few, and some types look related to those in other vertebrates.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is small enough that motif, backbone, and influential-node analyses can be tied to identified neurons and behavior.
ocar.challenge: Most network studies treat chemical synapses and gap junctions as the same edges, collapsing distinct motif families.
ocar.action: In Journal of Complex Networks (2023), Liu, Yuan, Zhao, Gu, Huo, Li, and Fang separate chemical and electrical contacts, expand three-neuron motif families, then extract a motif-based backbone and an influential-neuron ranking.
ocar.resolution: The backbone they extract is described as controlling an essential motor behavior. Motif-based influential neurons are argued to be more functionally informative than standard rankings; Table 2 lists influential indices (e.g., AVEL/AVER/AVBL/AVBR/AVAL/AVAR at 1000).
ocar.future_work: The discussion frames the methods as a biologically interpretable exploration of neural-network structure; generalization beyond C. elegans is not demonstrated in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring is usually drawn as one kind of arrow, but chemical synapses and electrical gap junctions are different. Splitting them reveals new repeating triangles and a “backbone” the authors say is important for movement, plus a ranked list of influential cells.
summaries.intermediate: In J. Complex Networks (2023; cnad013), Liu and colleagues expand neural motifs by distinguishing chemical synapses from gap junctions in C. elegans. A motif-based algorithm extracts a backbone circuit tied to essential motor behavior and another ranks influential neurons, which they contrast with existing methods as more functionally informative. An influential-index table highlights command-like neurons (e.g., AVA, AVB, AVE at the top of the scale they use).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s discussion is brief; quantitative motif-enrichment statistics and the exact motor behavior of the backbone are not fully specified here. Influential index is a custom score (table color scale), not a standard centrality with published units. Treating chemical versus electrical edges is the methodological claim; whether the expanded motifs are computationally used by the worm is interpretive.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring is usually drawn as one kind of arrow, but chemical synapses and electrical gap junctions are different. Splitting them reveals new repeating triangles and a “backbone” the authors say is important for movement, plus a ranked list of influential cells.

ocar.opportunity: Monosynaptic G-deleted rabies tracing is widely used, but typical convergence indices do not say what fraction of synapses or input cells are labeled.
ocar.challenge: Whether labeling efficiency depends on postsynaptic cell type or distance from the soma was unknown at synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: In eLife (2023), Patiño, Lagos, Patne, Miyazaki, Bhamidipati, Collman, and Callaway use a rabies construct that labels pre- and postsynaptic specializations in mouse V1 under typical AAV helper and EnvA+ RVdG conditions, quantified at 7 days post-infection.
ocar.resolution: About 40% of first-order excitatory synaptic contacts onto L4 pyramidal, Sst, and Vip starters were labeled (similar across those types), with no difference by subcellular location. They estimate input-neuron fraction ≳30% and unitary per-synapse spread probability ~28%.
ocar.future_work: Results are for one titer/strain/time point; shorter survival might still bias proximal synapses. Shared inputs and multi-contact axons slightly inflate synaptic fraction relative to unitary spread.

summaries.beginner: A popular virus that hops one synapse backward does not label every input. In mouse visual cortex, under typical conditions, it marked about two in five excitatory contacts, and that fraction did not depend on cell type or how far the synapse sat from the cell body.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2023; e89297), Patiño and colleagues measure synaptic fraction (SF) of monosynaptic rabies spread in mouse primary visual cortex. With their AAV helpers and EnvA+ RVdG, SF is about 40% onto L4 excitatory, Sst, and Vip starters, independent of dendritic location at 7 dpi. They relate SF to input fraction (IF ≳ 0.30) and unitary efficiency U ≈ 28%, discussing multiple contacts per axon. The editor’s evaluation calls the quantification convincing for visual cortical neurons under these conditions.
summaries.advanced: Efficiency is not a universal constant of rabies tracing; glycoprotein level and CI were already known to move labeling. “Do not determine efficiency” applies to the matched conditions and cell types tested, not all brain areas. Distal-versus-proximal equality is at 7 days; earlier times may differ (Nassi and Callaway 2006). Inhibitory-to-excitatory spread is not the measured set here (excitatory contacts).

plain_language_summary: A popular virus that hops one synapse backward does not label every input. In mouse visual cortex, under typical conditions, it marked about two in five excitatory contacts, and that fraction did not depend on cell type or how far the synapse sat from the cell body.

ocar.opportunity: Proprioceptive feedback must be gated by behavioral context so reflexes do not fight voluntary movement; presynaptic inhibition is a classic candidate mechanism.
ocar.challenge: Whether position- versus movement-encoding leg proprioceptors are suppressed differently during walking and grooming, and which VNC circuit does it, was unclear in Drosophila.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (version posted 11 May 2024), Dallmann, Luo, Agrawal, Chou, Cook, Brunton, and Tuthill combine calcium imaging in behaving flies, FANC connectomics, and imaging of candidate interneurons and descending inputs.
ocar.resolution: Position-encoding proprioceptor axons stay active across behaviors; movement-encoding axons are suppressed during walking and grooming via a repeated GABAergic interneuron motif driven mainly by descending neurons. Interneuron and descending activity tracks self-generated, not passive, leg movements.
ocar.future_work: They suggest testing whether the same logic applies to mammalian Ia versus II muscle-spindle afferents. FANC proofreading contributions are acknowledged.

summaries.beginner: When a fly walks, it still needs to know where its legs are, but it may not want a flood of movement signals. This study finds a spinal-cord-like circuit that turns down movement sensors during self-made steps, using a prediction from the brain.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2023.10.20.563322; May 2024 version), Dallmann and colleagues show differential proprioceptive gating in Drosophila: position-encoding axons remain active, movement-encoding axons are suppressed during walking and grooming. Connectomics identifies local GABAergic interneurons that presynaptically inhibit movement-encoding terminals, with descending neurons as their main inputs—consistent with predictive inhibition/efference copy. Calcium imaging confirms interneurons and descending cells correlate with active, not passive, movements.
summaries.advanced: Causal necessity of the identified interneuron class for behavior is supported by the circuit-and-imaging package in the paper; the selected extract’s conclusion is mechanistic rather than a single optogenetic statistic. Analogy to mammalian spindles is explicit future work. Catalog year 2023 is the original posting; this extract is the 2024 update.

plain_language_summary: When a fly walks, it still needs to know where its legs are, but it may not want a flood of movement signals. This study finds a spinal-cord-like circuit that turns down movement sensors during self-made steps, using a prediction from the brain.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM now gives nanometer morphologies of mushroom-body output neurons; combining that with physiology can test whether synapse location on the dendrite matters for memory readout.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian neurons often need active dendritic strategies for “synaptic democracy”; it was unknown whether a fly MBON integrates its many Kenyon-cell inputs equally.
ocar.action: In eLife (2023), Hafez, Escribano, Ziegler, Hirtz, Niebur, and Pielage build a model of MBON-α3 using EM architecture, 948 presynaptic Kenyon cells, and patch-clamp membrane properties.
ocar.resolution: MBON-α3 is electrotonically compact: simulated odor-like synaptic input robustly drives spiking with little dependence on synapse location, so sparse, stochastic KC connectivity can store many memories without precise anatomical addressing. The editor highlights this as synaptic democracy via passive dendrites.
ocar.future_work: Validity is argued for passive models of fly circuits; it does not claim mammalian pyramidal neurons work the same way.

summaries.beginner: A fly memory-output cell receives almost a thousand input wires. A detailed model says those inputs count roughly equally no matter where they sit on the tree, so the circuit can use messy, random connections and still learn many smells.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2023; e77578), Hafez and colleagues combine EM morphology of MBON-α3, synapses from 948 Kenyon cells, and patch-clamp parameters in a realistic compartmental model. The neuron is electrotonically compact; sparse KC input drives spiking, and location on the arbor has minimal effect (synaptic democracy). That architecture supports storing many associations with stochastic connectivity. Reviewers contrast this passive strategy with larger mammalian neurons that use active dendritic mechanisms.
summaries.advanced: Results are for one MBON type (α3), not all MBONs. “948 presynaptic KCs” is the reconstructed complement used, not a claim about every fly. Compactness is a modeling conclusion from measured properties plus EM, not in vivo voltage throughout the arbor. Preprint dates to 2020; published 14 March 2023.

plain_language_summary: A fly memory-output cell receives almost a thousand input wires. A detailed model says those inputs count roughly equally no matter where they sit on the tree, so the circuit can use messy, random connections and still learn many smells.

ocar.opportunity: Hard X-ray holographic nano-tomography (XNH) images thick samples quickly with intrinsic alignment, a potential shortcut around serial-section EM, but resolution is too low for easy membrane segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Cross-modality translation from X-ray to EM-like appearance must preserve membranes and quantify uncertainty if it is to help connectomics pipelines.
ocar.action: At ISBI 2023 (arXiv:2303.00882), Li, Meirovitch, Kuan, Phelps, Pacureanu, Lee, Shavit, and Mi propose X-Ray2EM, an uncertainty-aware 3D cGAN (3D Pix2Pix-style generator plus PatchGAN) with a frozen 2D U-Net segmentation head pretrained on Kasthuri mouse-cortex membranes.
ocar.resolution: They translate XNH to EM-like volumes with improved membrane segmentation quality relative to the X-ray domain, aiming at simpler X-ray-based connectomics. Paired data are ssTEM versus XNH (Kuan–Phelps 2020 Lee lab release).
ocar.future_work: Training details (128×128×64 crops, 100 epochs, loss weights) are methods, not a claim of synapse-resolution X-ray connectomes. Public benchmark EM differs in domain from their X-Ray2EM pair (Figure 5).

summaries.beginner: X-rays can scan thick brain tissue faster than slicing it for electron microscopy, but the pictures are blurrier. This model tries to paint EM-like membranes onto X-ray volumes so computers can trace cells more easily.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE ISBI (2023; DOI 10.1109/ISBI53787.2023.10230759), Li and colleagues present X-Ray2EM, a 3D uncertainty-aware reconstruction network mapping X-ray holographic nano-tomography to EM-like images. A U-Net segmentation network is pretrained on Kasthuri ssSEM membranes, then frozen while a 3D Pix2Pix-style generator is trained with NLL, GAN, and segmentation losses. They visualize membrane probability maps along X–Y and Y–Z. Data: Lee lab XNH/EM pair and a public EM benchmark.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is heavy on training hyperparameters; headline Dice/F1 scores are not in the captured text. Domain gap between public EM and X-Ray2EM data is explicitly illustrated. XNH is not claimed to replace synaptic-resolution EM. Catalog methods include X-ray microscopy and volume EM as the two domains.

plain_language_summary: X-rays can scan thick brain tissue faster than slicing it for electron microscopy, but the pictures are blurrier. This model tries to paint EM-like membranes onto X-ray volumes so computers can trace cells more easily.

ocar.opportunity: Layer 4 of primary sensory cortex is the main thalamic recipient, but average connectivity has hidden higher-order inhibitory logic.
ocar.challenge: Feedforward inhibition is known functionally, yet a synapse-level picture of which interneurons the thalamus drives, and how they target excitatory subtypes and each other, was missing.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (1 June 2022), Hua, Loomba, Pawlak, Laserstein, Boergens, Kerr, and Helmstaedter reconstruct about one quarter of the mouse C2 barrel through L4 (and parts of L3/L5A) with SBEM after in vivo two-photon imaging.
ocar.resolution: Thalamic input drives a specific interneuron subset; those cells target spiny stellate versus star pyramidal neurons with subtype specificity and form a directed, thalamus-driven disinhibitory network, creating differential windows of opportunity for excitatory types depending on thalamic timing and strength.
ocar.future_work: They call this a first connectomic description of thalamus-driven L4 inhibition; excitatory intracortical networks are left for future work to test whether equal precision is general in cortex.

summaries.beginner: When a whisker signal hits cortex, it does not only excite cells; it also turns selected inhibitory cells on in a precise pattern. Mapping those connections in a mouse barrel, the authors find a disinhibitory loop that could open different time windows for two kinds of excitatory neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2022; 10.1101/2022.06.01.494290), Hua, Loomba, and colleagues use SBEM connectomics on ~¼ of the mouse S1 C2 barrel across L4. Thalamic axons preferentially drive a subset of interneurons that inhibit excitatory subtypes differentially and also disinhibit in a directed, thalamus-driven network. The proposed computation is temporal windows for spiny stellates versus star pyramids. Tissue was previously imaged in vivo with two-photon GCaMP in Scnn1a-Cre mice.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s “Outlook” is short; numeric synapse counts and statistical tests are not in the selected text. Volume is a fraction of one barrel, not whole S1. “Unknown degree of specialization” is the authors’ claim relative to prior average connectivity. Methods pages detail virus and imaging but are not results.

plain_language_summary: When a whisker signal hits cortex, it does not only excite cells; it also turns selected inhibitory cells on in a precise pattern. Mapping those connections in a mouse barrel, the authors find a disinhibitory loop that could open different time windows for two kinds of excitatory neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes constrain detailed circuit models, but mapping synapses onto physiological weights and integration rules remains hard.
ocar.challenge: A new experimental study of a fruit-fly pathway reports how connectivity relates to physiology; the field needs a concise interpretation of what that implies for models.
ocar.action: In a Current Biology dispatch (2022), Ganguly and Litwin-Kumar discuss that study’s relationship between synaptic wiring and physiology in a Drosophila pathway.
ocar.resolution: The catalog abstract states the work describes this relationship for a fly neural pathway and suggests a path forward for future models. A fragment of matching text in the file mentions synaptic democracy within but independence across axonal and dendritic arbors in the Liu et al. Drosophila connectome study, implying an intermediate abstraction between point neurons and full multi-compartment models.
ocar.future_work: Understanding how those two input sources interact may reveal new computational principles still amenable to theory.

summaries.beginner: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing how the circuit computes. This short commentary explains a fly study that links synapses to physiology and sketches how modelers might use that link.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022; DOI 10.1016/j.cub.2021.12.037), Ganguly and Litwin-Kumar dispatch on relating connectomes to physiology, focusing on a fruit-fly pathway (the catalog abstract). They present the study as a guide for models constrained by the Drosophila connectome. Where the matching fragment is readable, they highlight synaptic democracy within arbors but independence across axon versus dendrite, suggesting gated, two-stream abstractions rather than pure point neurons.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the selected text opens with references from a different Current Biology dispatch on Arabidopsis pavement-cell morphogenesis; only a later fragment matches the Ganguly & Litwin-Kumar fly-connectome dispatch (citing Liu et al.). Summaries therefore rely on the catalog abstract plus that fragment; quantitative physiology from the discussed study is not in a clean extract.

plain_language_summary: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as knowing how the circuit computes. This short commentary explains a fly study that links synapses to physiology and sketches how modelers might use that link.

ocar.opportunity: 3D nuclei instance segmentation is routine in annotated EM but costly to label in new modalities such as expansion microscopy (ExM).
ocar.challenge: Generalist pretrained models and two-step translate-then-segment pipelines underuse unlabeled target images and can break instance boundaries.
ocar.action: On arXiv (2022), Lauenburg, Lin, Zhang, dos Santos, Huang, Arganda-Carreras, Boyden, Pfister, and Wei propose CySGAN, jointly training CycleGAN translation and instance segmentation with extra self-supervised and segmentation-adversarial losses, benchmarked on labeled EM to unlabeled ExM nuclei (NucExM dataset released).
ocar.resolution: CySGAN outperforms Cellpose, StarDist, and sequential CycleGAN+segmentation; it beats the second-best (CycleGAN+Segm, IX→IY) by 5.7 percentage points. On the optimized NucExM volume V1, AP-50 is 0.927, dropping to 0.761 without augmentations and 0.878 without semi-supervised losses.
ocar.future_work: They flag target domains whose instance geometry differs strongly from the source as an important open direction.

summaries.beginner: Labeling every nucleus in a new kind of microscope image is slow. This method learns to both paint one image type into another and find each nucleus, using unlabeled examples of the new type, and it beats doing those two steps separately.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2022; 2204.03082), Lauenburg and colleagues introduce CySGAN for unlabeled-modality instance segmentation. The benchmark is 3D neuronal nuclei: annotated EM as source, unlabeled ExM as target, with a new densely annotated ExM set (NucExM). Unified translation-plus-segmentation outperforms generalists (Cellpose, StarDist) and sequential translation–segmentation. Ablations show data augmentation and semi-supervised target losses are essential (AP-50 0.927 vs. large drops when removed). Code and data: connectomics-bazaar.github.io/proj/CySGAN/.
summaries.advanced: AP-50 figures are for the stated NucExM splits (train on V1, infer V2 in the sequential/CySGAN comparison). Star-convex priors (StarDist) are said to overlap and miss boundaries. The method assumes source and target instances are similar enough to share a segmentation representation. NSF/NIH funding is acknowledged; Boyden is a coauthor on the ExM side.

plain_language_summary: Labeling every nucleus in a new kind of microscope image is slow. This method learns to both paint one image type into another and find each nucleus, using unlabeled examples of the new type, and it beats doing those two steps separately.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans klinotaxis (gradual steering up a salt gradient) coexists with a random walk; a connectome-based model that produces both would constrain mechanisms.
ocar.challenge: ASEL/R cannot read a spatial gradient directly (the worm lies on its side); ASEL’s all-or-none depolarization had not been in prior sensory models, and random walking was often added externally rather than generated by synapses.
ocar.action: In Scientific Reports (2022), Chen, Feng, Su, Su, and Wang evolve a connectome-constrained network with a new ASEL all-or-none sensory model, then introduce “liquid synapses” whose stochasticity generates autonomous random walking.
ocar.resolution: Klinotaxis emerges from the evolved network with a plausible steering mechanism; liquid synapses produce random walk from the circuit itself. Simulated ablations are reported as consistent with biological conclusions.
ocar.future_work: Liquid synapses are a modeling hypothesis inspired by biological synaptic stochasticity, not a newly measured synapse class. They analogize to Drosophila larval spontaneous search after sensory block.

summaries.beginner: Worms climb salt gradients while still wandering. This simulation uses the worm’s wiring, a more realistic nose cell, and noisy synapses to get both steering and random walking from the network instead of adding wandering by hand.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2022; 10.1038/s41598-022-06988-w), Chen and colleagues build a C. elegans klinotaxis model with an ASEL all-or-none sensory stage (claimed first) plus ASER, evolve the network, and then add stochastic “liquid synapses” so a random walk is generated internally. They argue the klinotaxis mechanism resembles, but refines, prior minimal models, and that ablation simulations match biology. The paper is positioned as behavioral simulation plus mechanistic hypothesis.
summaries.advanced: “Fairly consistent” ablation results are the authors’ comparison to literature, not a full experimental replication. Liquid synapses are a proposed stochastic synapse model. Connectome completeness cites ~302 neurons and >7000 connections as background, not a new reconstruction. Evolutionary training means the weights are optimized for the task, not taken as measured physiological weights.

plain_language_summary: Worms climb salt gradients while still wandering. This simulation uses the worm’s wiring, a more realistic nose cell, and noisy synapses to get both steering and random walking from the network instead of adding wandering by hand.
